Summary: Jesus' closing command to the parable of the Good Samaritan, stated as a command and not merely a moral: go, and do thou likewise.
Application: The lawyer asked who his neighbour was; Jesus reverses the question into action. The Samaritan's mercy — binding wounds, paying the cost — becomes the hearer's assignment. This row is included because Jesus states it as a command, not because a parable's moral was assumed to be one.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to turn neighbour-love from a definition into costly action toward whoever lies wounded in the road.
Function: The lawyer asked who his neighbour was; Jesus turned the question into an assignment. This comes from the New Testament, not from Sinai, so the old threefold division does not apply to it. Its goal, on the TRADITIONAL reading, was to turn neighbour-love from a definition into costly action toward whoever lies wounded in the road. The evil it addressed was love kept theoretical — defined, debated, and never done. It restrained that evil with the Samaritan's mercy: binding wounds, paying the cost, and the word, go, and do thou likewise.
